notes:
Chapter overview

Contributions of Perarignar Anna examines his rise from Kanchipuram teacher and journalist to Dravidian organiser, DMK founder, parliamentarian and chief minister who converted social-movement demands into democratic government policy.

Early life & PeriyarPrint, theatre & cinemaDMK & mobilisationLanguage, federalism & ParliamentGovernment & legacy
Birth, Family, Education and Early Career

Anna’s early life in Kanchipuram, education at Pachaiyappa’s College, brief teaching career and exceptional oratory prepared him for mass democratic leadership.

Birth

Conjeevaram Natarajan Annadurai was born on:

  • 15 September 1909
  • At Kanchipuram
  • In the Madras Presidency

He became popularly known as:

  • C. N. Annadurai
  • C.N.A.
  • Anna
  • Arignar Anna
  • Perarignar Anna

“Anna” means:

  • Elder brother

The title reflected the accessible and affectionate public image he developed among supporters.

Parents and Family

His parents were:

  • Natarajan
  • Bangaru Ammal

He was brought up in a socially modest family environment.

His early experiences exposed him to:

  • Social inequality
  • Caste distinctions
  • Economic hardship
  • Educational barriers
Marriage

Anna married:

  • Rani Ammal

The couple had no biological children but raised children from within the extended family.

School Education

Anna received his early education in Kanchipuram.

He later worked for a short period in the municipal administration before pursuing higher education.

Pachaiyappa’s College

He studied at:

  • Pachaiyappa’s College
  • Madras

His education included subjects connected with:

  • Economics
  • Politics
  • History
  • Public administration

His college years helped develop his interest in:

  • Debate
  • Public speaking
  • Literature
  • Social reform
  • Politics
Teaching Career

Anna worked briefly as a teacher.

Teaching strengthened his ability to:

  • Explain complex ideas simply
  • Engage younger audiences
  • Organise arguments
  • Speak in an accessible style
Development as an Orator

He became known for speeches marked by:

  • Clarity
  • Humour
  • Alliteration
  • Literary references
  • Logical organisation
  • Memorable comparisons
  • Direct audience interaction

His oratory became one of the principal instruments through which the Dravidian Movement reached ordinary people.

Historical Importance of His Background

Anna did not emerge from:

  • A wealthy landed family
  • A hereditary political dynasty
  • Colonial administrative privilege

His rise through:

  • Education
  • Journalism
  • Public speaking
  • Organisation
  • Electoral politics

represented the expanding political participation of non-elite social groups. Anna was born in Kanchipuram on 15 September 1909 and later became the founder of the DMK and chief minister of Madras State.

Entry into the Justice Party and Association with Periyar

His entry into the Justice Party and association with Periyar linked non-Brahmin representation and Self-Respect ideas with a younger electoral political strategy.

Entry into Public Politics

Anna became involved in the non-Brahmin political current during the 1930s.

He was attracted to issues such as:

  • Communal representation
  • Educational opportunity
  • Social equality
  • Opposition to caste monopoly
  • Provincial rights
Justice Party

He joined the political tradition represented by the:

  • Justice Party

The party had been founded in 1916 to advance:

  • Non-Brahmin representation
  • Public-employment access
  • Educational opportunity
  • Provincial political participation

Anna did not found the Justice Party.

He entered it during a later phase of its development.

Association with Periyar

Anna came under the influence of:

  • E. V. Ramasamy Periyar
  • Self-Respect ideology
  • Rationalist criticism
  • Anti-caste propaganda

He became one of Periyar’s prominent younger associates.

Shared Positions

Anna and Periyar broadly agreed on:

  • Opposition to caste hierarchy
  • Social justice
  • Communal representation
  • Tamil linguistic dignity
  • Criticism of compulsory Hindi
  • Opposition to hereditary privilege
  • Need for social reform
Difference in Style

Even before their organisational separation, their styles differed.

Periyar
  • Direct iconoclasm
  • Harsh criticism
  • Non-electoral social revolution
  • Rejection of religious compromise
Anna
  • Persuasive oratory
  • Humour and literary communication
  • Electoral mobilisation
  • Greater accommodation of popular religious sentiment
Public Role

Anna became valuable to the movement because he could convert ideological arguments into:

  • Speeches
  • Essays
  • Plays
  • Dialogues
  • Short political slogans
Mentor–Disciple Relationship

Periyar was an important ideological mentor to Anna.

However, Anna did not remain merely an interpreter of Periyar.

He developed an independent political approach based upon:

  • Electoral democracy
  • Party organisation
  • Tamil mass culture
  • Parliamentary federalism
  • Gradual social reform
Historical Significance

The Periyar–Anna relationship connected two stages of the movement:

  • Non-electoral Self-Respect social revolution
  • Electoral Dravidian mass politics

Their later disagreement did not erase the strong ideological influence Periyar exercised on Anna’s early career.

Journalism, Publications and Political Education

Through Viduthalai, Dravida Nadu, Kanchi and English writing, Anna converted journalism into public political education and cadre training.

Journalism as Public Education

Anna treated journalism as a means to:

  • Educate supporters
  • Explain policies
  • Criticise governments
  • Train party cadres
  • Develop Tamil political vocabulary
Viduthalai

Anna worked in association with:

  • Viduthalai

The publication was connected with the Justice Party and later the Dravidar Kazhagam tradition.

His journalistic work helped him acquire experience in:

  • Editorial writing
  • Political criticism
  • Daily public communication
  • Movement organisation
Dravida Nadu

Anna founded and edited the Tamil weekly:

  • Dravida Nadu

It began publication in:

  • 1942

It became an important platform for:

  • Dravidian identity
  • Social justice
  • Tamil language
  • Political autonomy
  • Criticism of Congress
  • Organisational debate
Kanchi

He was also associated with the publication:

  • Kanchi

It carried:

  • Political commentary
  • Literary writing
  • Movement explanations
  • Responses to contemporary events
English Journalism

Anna wrote and spoke in English as well as Tamil.

This enabled him to present Dravidian arguments to:

  • National political audiences
  • Parliamentarians
  • English-educated readers
  • Critics outside Tamil Nadu
Writing Style

His prose was characterised by:

  • Short and forceful sentences
  • Wordplay
  • Historical comparisons
  • Questions and answers
  • Satire
  • Direct appeals
Political Education of Cadres

Anna used party publications to train followers in:

  • Public speaking
  • Social-justice arguments
  • Language policy
  • Federalism
  • Election work
  • Democratic opposition
Journalism and Internal Debate

Publications also allowed discussion of disagreements concerning:

  • Electoral participation
  • Dravida Nadu
  • Independence
  • Relations with Periyar
  • Party strategy
Contribution

Anna helped transform political journalism from elite commentary into a mass educational instrument.

His publications connected:

  • Ideology
  • Literature
  • Organisation
  • Electoral mobilisation
Literature, Theatre and Social Criticism

Anna’s plays, stories and essays transformed caste, class, labour, religion and women’s status into accessible social criticism.

Anna as a Writer

Anna wrote:

  • Plays
  • Novellas
  • Short stories
  • Political essays
  • Social criticism
  • Film scripts
  • Dialogues

His literary works were not separate from his politics.

They communicated ideas concerning:

  • Caste
  • Class
  • Religious hypocrisy
  • Women’s status
  • Labour
  • Social inequality
  • Rationalism
Major Plays and Literary Works

Important works associated with Anna include:

  • Velaikkari
  • Or Iravu
  • Sivaji Kanda Hindu Samrajyam
  • Needhi Devan Mayakkam
  • Chandrodayam
  • Sorgavasal
  • Kadhal Jothi
  • Pavayin Payanam

Important prose and polemical works included:

  • Ariya Mayai
  • Kambarasam
  • Panathottam
  • Romapuri Rani
  • Parvathi B.A.
  • Rangoon Radha

The classification of some works varies because several appeared first as:

  • Serial fiction
  • Stage plays
  • Political essays
  • Later film adaptations
Velaikkari

Velaikkari focused on questions such as:

  • Class exploitation
  • Wealth inequality
  • Labour dignity
  • Religious hypocrisy
  • Social injustice

Its message challenged the belief that wealth or status automatically produced moral superiority.

Or Iravu

Or Iravu depicted:

  • Poverty
  • Family separation
  • Social inequality
  • Urban hardship
  • Moral contradictions

The story takes place substantially within the course of one night.

Sivaji Kanda Hindu Samrajyam

This play examined:

  • Caste hierarchy
  • Ritual authority
  • Coronation
  • Brahminical recognition of kingship

It presented the contradiction between military achievement and ritual status.

Needhi Devan Mayakkam

The work questioned literary and moral judgement.

It used dramatic argument to re-examine established interpretations of:

  • Justice
  • Epic characters
  • Literary authority
Literature as Social Intervention

Anna did not write only for literary elites.

His works were designed for:

  • Public performance
  • Political education
  • Popular reading
  • Movement fundraising
  • Cadre mobilisation
Accessible Tamil

He blended:

  • Literary Tamil
  • Spoken expression
  • Humour
  • Rhetoric
  • Political vocabulary

This helped make modern political ideas accessible to large audiences.

Literary Contribution

Anna’s literary importance lies not merely in the number of works he produced.

He helped create a form of Tamil political literature in which:

  • Dialogue became propaganda.
  • Drama became social criticism.
  • Entertainment became political education.

His major stage and screen works included Velaikkari, Or Iravu, Nallathambi and Sorgavasal.

Cinema and the Democratisation of Political Communication

Cinema carried Anna’s reform vocabulary to mass audiences and helped integrate theatre, actors, political dialogue and electoral mobilisation.

Cinema as a Mass Medium

Anna recognised that cinema could reach:

  • Urban workers
  • Rural audiences
  • Women
  • Young people
  • People with limited literacy

Cinema therefore became a major medium of Dravidian political communication.

Film Contributions

Films connected with Anna’s stories, screenplays or dialogues included:

  • Nallathambi
  • Velaikkari
  • Or Iravu
  • Sorgavasal
  • Rangoon Radha
  • Nallavan Vazhvan

The precise nature of his contribution differed from film to film and included:

  • Story
  • Screenplay
  • Dialogue
  • Adaptation of stage work
Political Dialogue

Anna’s film writing introduced themes such as:

  • Social equality
  • Labour rights
  • Rationalism
  • Criticism of exploitation
  • Opposition to blind ritual
  • Dignity of ordinary people
Cinema and Spoken Tamil

Film dialogues allowed political language to enter:

  • Households
  • Tea shops
  • Workplaces
  • Village gatherings
  • Public memory
Relationship with Actors

The Dravidian movement developed links with actors and theatre personalities.

Artists became:

  • Speakers
  • Campaigners
  • Fundraisers
  • Candidates
  • Cultural symbols
N. S. Krishnan and K. R. Ramasamy

Artists such as:

  • N. S. Krishnan
  • K. R. Ramasamy

were associated in different ways with reform-oriented theatre and Dravidian political culture.

M. R. Radha

M. R. Radha’s stage performances contributed to:

  • Rationalist criticism
  • Anti-caste messages
  • Social satire
M. G. Ramachandran

M.G. Ramachandran later became a major popular face of the DMK.

His screen image helped expand the party’s reach.

Sivaji Ganesan

Sivaji Ganesan was also connected with the early Dravidian theatrical environment before later political differences.

His stage name “Sivaji” became associated with his performance in a play connected with Anna’s writing.

Contribution

Anna helped create a model in which cinema was not merely used to advertise a party.

It was used to build:

  • Political vocabulary
  • Emotional identification
  • Leadership image
  • Social-reform consciousness
Long-Term Effect

The integration of:

  • Cinema
  • Politics
  • Oratory
  • Welfare symbolism

became a distinctive feature of Tamil Nadu’s later political culture.

Role in Dravidar Kazhagam and Ideological Development

Anna contributed to the 1944 transformation into Dravidar Kazhagam while increasingly emphasising democratic participation, communication and youth organisation.

Formation of Dravidar Kazhagam

At the Salem conference of:

  • 27 August 1944

the Justice Party was transformed into:

  • Dravidar Kazhagam
  • DK

Anna played an important role in the organisational and ideological transition.

Anna Resolution

The Salem changes are often associated with resolutions promoted by Anna.

They included calls for members to:

  • Renounce colonial titles
  • Withdraw from nominated offices
  • Remove caste suffixes
  • Emphasise social reform
  • Reorganise under a Dravidian identity
From Elite Party to Social Movement

The transformation shifted emphasis from:

  • Colonial constitutional politics
  • Elite representation
  • Government office

towards:

  • Anti-caste propaganda
  • Rationalism
  • Dravidian identity
  • Social revolution
  • Mass mobilisation
Anna’s Ideological Position

Anna accepted many major DK principles but gave greater importance to:

  • Communication
  • Democratic participation
  • Youth mobilisation
  • Organisational expansion
  • Future electoral action
Indian Independence

Periyar viewed the transfer of power in 1947 critically because he believed that:

  • Caste domination remained.
  • Social freedom had not been achieved.
  • Political power was transferred to Indian elites.

Anna adopted a more positive interpretation of independence.

He considered the end of colonial rule an important achievement even though social reform remained incomplete.

August 15 Disagreement

The difference over whether 15 August 1947 should be treated as:

  • A day of mourning
  • Or a day of political achievement

revealed a growing strategic division.

Black Shirt Question

Anna accepted protest symbolism but was less inclined to make a uniform or single style of protest compulsory for all supporters.

Emerging Difference

The disagreement was not simply personal.

It concerned:

  • Meaning of independence
  • Election participation
  • Organisational democracy
  • Generational leadership
  • Methods of social reform
Differences with Periyar and Formation of the DMK

Differences over elections, independence, succession and strategy culminated in the 1949 formation of the DMK; the Maniammai marriage intensified but did not solely cause the split.

Background to the Split

By the late 1940s, differences had developed between Periyar and younger DK leaders.

The principal issues included:

  • Electoral politics
  • Organisational democracy
  • Political independence
  • Leadership succession
  • Pace and method of reform
  • Relationship with ordinary religious believers
Periyar’s Position

Periyar believed elections encouraged:

  • Opportunism
  • Caste mobilisation
  • Desire for office
  • Ideological compromise

He preferred DK to remain a non-electoral social movement.

Anna’s Position

Anna believed political power could be used to:

  • Pass social-reform laws
  • Protect reservation
  • Advance Tamil
  • Implement welfare
  • Strengthen state rights
Marriage to Maniammai

Periyar’s marriage to Maniammai in:

  • 1949

intensified the organisational dispute.

Some younger leaders questioned:

  • Leadership succession
  • Property administration
  • Internal consultation

However, the marriage was not the sole cause of the split.

Formation of DMK

The Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam was founded in:

  • 1949

Anna became its principal founder and general secretary.

The party’s formation was publicly announced at a meeting in:

  • Robinson Park
  • Royapuram
  • Madras
Meaning of the Name

Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam may be rendered broadly as:

  • Dravidian Progressive Federation

The use of “Munnetra” or progress indicated a forward-looking political programme.

Relationship with DK

Anna initially avoided presenting DMK as an enemy of DK.

Both shared several social objectives.

The major institutional distinction was:

DK
  • Non-electoral
  • Periyar-led
  • Social-revolutionary organisation
DMK
  • Electoral orientation
  • Anna-led
  • Political party
  • Mass organisation
Organisational Symbolism

The DMK adopted:

  • Black and red colours

These represented broadly:

Black
  • Existing oppression
  • Social darkness
Red
  • Change
  • Awakening
  • Progress
Contribution

Anna’s founding of DMK converted Dravidian social ideology into a durable electoral movement.

This altered Tamil politics by creating a major alternative to Congress rule.

Party Organisation, Oratory and Mass Mobilisation

Anna built a cadre-based party through branches, conferences, disciplined public speaking, cultural programmes and the values of duty, dignity and discipline.

Anna’s Oratory

Anna was regarded as one of the leading Tamil and English orators of his period.

His speeches used:

  • Alliteration
  • Antithesis
  • Humour
  • Historical analogy
  • Short stories
  • Literary quotations
  • Questions
  • Memorable slogans
Accessible Leadership

He cultivated the image of:

  • Anna
  • Elder brother

This differed from a distant or highly ceremonial political-leadership style.

Cadre-Based Organisation

The DMK developed:

  • Local branches
  • District organisations
  • Youth groups
  • Student networks
  • Women’s participation
  • Cultural troupes
  • Reading rooms
Public Meetings

Meetings often combined:

  • Political speeches
  • Drama
  • Songs
  • Poetry
  • Humour
  • Film personalities

This made political activity a form of mass culture.

Party Conferences

DMK conferences served to:

  • Pass resolutions
  • Train cadres
  • demonstrate organisational strength
  • Debate strategy
  • Mobilise funds
Election Fundraising

Anna encouraged small public contributions.

This helped create the impression that the party belonged to:

  • Ordinary workers
  • Small traders
  • Students
  • Lower-middle-class supporters
Kadamai, Kanniyam, Kattupaadu

Anna popularised the organisational values:

  • Kadamai — Duty
  • Kanniyam — Dignity
  • Kattupaadu — Discipline

These principles were intended to guide party cadres.

Party Discipline

He emphasised that mass enthusiasm had to be combined with:

  • Organisational order
  • Public responsibility
  • Respectful conduct
  • Collective decision-making
Democratic Communication

Anna often answered critics through:

  • Public debate
  • Essays
  • Parliamentary speech
  • Humour rather than personal abuse
Contribution

He transformed the movement from a reformist intellectual network into a large-scale political organisation capable of:

  • Contesting elections
  • Forming alliances
  • Governing the state
  • Surviving leadership transitions
Social Justice, Caste Reform and Inclusive Politics

He connected reservation and caste reform with inclusive electoral coalitions, public policy and a less confrontational approach to personal religious belief.

Social Justice

Anna retained social justice as a central Dravidian objective.

He supported:

  • Reservation
  • Educational access
  • Public-employment representation
  • Advancement of backward communities
  • Removal of caste inequality
From Anti-Caste Propaganda to Public Policy

Anna’s contribution lay in connecting social-reform arguments with:

  • Legislative action
  • Government policy
  • Electoral manifestos
  • Administrative implementation
Self-Respect

He accepted self-respect as a foundation of:

  • Human dignity
  • Social equality
  • Marriage reform
  • Political participation
Caste Identity

Anna opposed caste-based superiority.

He also recognised that caste could not be removed immediately by declaration alone.

Government had to address:

  • Educational inequality
  • Employment exclusion
  • Social discrimination
  • Lack of representation
Inclusive Political Language

Anna’s rhetoric was generally less confrontational towards individual social groups than Periyar’s.

He attempted to build a broad alliance including:

  • Backward classes
  • Scheduled Castes
  • Muslims
  • Christians
  • Workers
  • Students
  • Tamil cultural groups
  • Some progressive members of traditionally privileged communities
One Community, One God

Anna sometimes invoked the Tamil expression:

  • Ondre Kulam, Oruvane Devan

It may be understood as:

  • One community
  • One God

The expression was associated with Thirumoolar.

Anna used it to communicate:

  • Human unity
  • Social equality
  • Religious accommodation
Difference from Periyar

Periyar promoted explicit atheism.

Anna placed greater political emphasis on:

  • Opposition to religious exploitation
  • Equality among believers
  • Tolerance of private faith

This enabled the DMK to appeal to people who accepted social reform but remained religious.

Social Coalition and Limitations

The DMK’s broad coalition expanded representation.

However, electoral mobilisation did not automatically remove:

  • Caste voting
  • Dominant-caste influence
  • Dalit exclusion
  • Gender inequality

Anna’s inclusive politics reduced ideological isolation but required compromise.

Tamil Language, Cultural Identity and Literary Advancement

Anna made Tamil a modern democratic public language while combining cultural pride, accessible prose, classical references and openness to English knowledge.

Tamil as a Public Language

Anna worked to expand Tamil in:

  • Politics
  • Administration
  • Education
  • Journalism
  • Theatre
  • Cinema
  • Public speaking
Linguistic Dignity

He opposed the belief that Tamil was inferior to:

  • Sanskrit
  • Hindi
  • English

He presented Tamil as a language with:

  • Ancient literature
  • Independent grammar
  • Historical continuity
  • Modern political capacity
Accessible Tamil

Anna did not restrict Tamil pride to highly classical language.

He developed a public style that combined:

  • Literary richness
  • Spoken accessibility
  • Modern political vocabulary
  • Humour
Cultural Democratisation

His language allowed people without advanced classical training to participate in discussions of:

  • History
  • Government
  • Social reform
  • Federalism
  • Economics
Tamil Identity and Dravidian Identity

Anna used both identities.

Dravidian Identity
  • Broader social and linguistic framework
  • Anti-caste and South Indian political origin
Tamil Identity
  • Tamil language
  • Tamil-speaking territory
  • Tamil cultural pride

As linguistic states developed, Anna’s politics became increasingly centred upon Tamil Nadu.

Tamil Literature

Anna drew upon:

  • Sangam works
  • Thirukkural
  • Silappathikaram
  • Tamil devotional and ethical literature
  • Modern Tamil writers

He selectively used literary sources to support:

  • Equality
  • Good governance
  • Social responsibility
  • Linguistic pride
Opposition to Cultural Exclusiveness

Tamil cultural pride, in Anna’s politics, was intended to strengthen dignity.

It did not require the rejection of:

  • English knowledge
  • International culture
  • Democratic exchange
  • Other Indian languages
Contribution

Anna helped make Tamil language and identity central to democratic mass politics without confining them entirely to academic or literary institutions.

Anti-Hindi Politics and the Two-Language Principle

His opposition concerned compulsory Hindi and unequal opportunity, leading to the Tamil–English two-language policy under his government.

Background

Language became a major political issue because it affected:

  • Education
  • Union government employment
  • Administration
  • Competitive examinations
  • Cultural status
  • Centre–State relations
Opposition to Compulsory Hindi

Anna opposed:

  • Compulsory Hindi instruction
  • Exclusive Hindi official dominance
  • Linguistic inequality in employment
  • Cultural centralisation
Opposition to Hindi Imposition

Anna distinguished between:

  • Voluntary learning of a language
  • Compulsory imposition through state authority

The principal political objection concerned compulsion.

Early Anti-Hindi Movement

Anna participated in the Anti-Hindi movement associated with:

  • Periyar
  • Justice Party
  • Dravidian activists

during the late 1930s.

Official-Language Question

The Constitution provided for Hindi in Devanagari script as the Union’s official language, while English continued for an initial period.

The prospect of reducing English after:

  • 26 January 1965

created fear in non-Hindi-speaking states.

Anna’s Argument

He argued that exclusive Hindi dominance would give Hindi-speaking citizens an unequal advantage in:

  • Union examinations
  • Administration
  • Employment
  • Political influence
1965 Agitation

Tamil Nadu witnessed major anti-Hindi protests in:

  • 1965

Students played a central role.

The protests included:

  • Demonstrations
  • Strikes
  • Arrests
  • Violence in some places
  • Deaths and self-immolations
Anna’s Role

Anna and the DMK politically opposed Hindi imposition.

However, he also appealed for discipline and attempted to prevent uncontrolled violence.

Tamil and English

Anna supported the continuation of:

  • Tamil at the state level
  • English as a link language

English was considered useful because it:

  • Did not give one Indian linguistic region exclusive advantage.
  • Connected India with international knowledge.
  • Supported higher education and employment.
Two-Language Policy

Under Anna’s government, Tamil Nadu adopted the two-language approach centred on:

  • Tamil
  • English

The policy rejected compulsory Hindi in the state-school framework.

Contribution

Anna transformed opposition to Hindi imposition into a broader defence of:

  • Linguistic equality
  • Federalism
  • Equal employment opportunity
  • Tamil dignity

The two-language policy established under his government became a durable feature of Tamil Nadu’s educational politics.

Dravida Nadu, Federalism and State Autonomy

Anna shifted from the separate Dravida Nadu demand to constitutional federalism, regional dignity and state autonomy within India.

Dravida Nadu Demand

During the earlier phase of his career, Anna supported the demand for:

  • Dravida Nadu

The proposed political unit was associated with:

  • South Indian linguistic regions
  • Opposition to North Indian dominance
  • Protection of Dravidian interests
  • Resistance to centralisation
Parliamentary Defence

After entering the Rajya Sabha, Anna openly defended the right to discuss Dravida Nadu.

He distinguished between:

  • Democratic advocacy
  • Violent rebellion
Change in Political Conditions

Several developments weakened the demand:

  • Formation of linguistic states
  • Separate political identities of Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam regions
  • India’s constitutional development
  • National-security concerns
  • Limited support outside Tamil Nadu
Sixteenth Constitutional Amendment

The constitutional and political environment changed after the:

  • Sino-Indian War of 1962
  • Sixteenth Constitutional Amendment of 1963

The amendment strengthened requirements connected with:

  • Sovereignty
  • Integrity of India
  • Oaths by candidates and representatives
Abandonment of Secession

The DMK formally abandoned the separate Dravida Nadu demand in:

  • 1963

Anna explained that although the demand was given up, the causes that had produced regional dissatisfaction had not necessarily disappeared.

Shift to Federalism

Anna increasingly emphasised:

  • State rights
  • Decentralisation
  • Linguistic equality
  • Financial fairness
  • Federal democracy
State Autonomy

His later politics sought greater state authority within India rather than separation from India.

“Unity” and “Uniformity”

Anna distinguished national unity from enforced uniformity.

India could remain united while allowing states to preserve:

  • Language
  • Culture
  • Policy preferences
  • Political autonomy
Contribution

Anna’s transition showed political adaptability.

He moved from separatist advocacy to constitutional federalism without abandoning:

  • Regional dignity
  • Opposition to central domination
  • State-level political power

His Rajya Sabha speeches became notable expressions of Dravidian identity, democratic dissent and regional rights.

Parliamentary Career and Democratic Opposition

His Rajya Sabha career nationalised Dravidian arguments about language, federalism, democratic dissent and regional economic imbalance.

Rajya Sabha

Anna became a member of the:

  • Rajya Sabha
  • In 1962

He served there until moving into state government following the 1967 election.

National Audience

Parliament gave Anna a platform to explain Dravidian politics to the rest of India.

He spoke on:

  • Federalism
  • Language
  • Dravida Nadu
  • Democracy
  • Economic inequality
  • State rights
  • National integration
Maiden Speech

His early Rajya Sabha speeches attracted attention because of:

  • Fluency in English
  • Wit
  • Logical argument
  • Open defence of regional identity
  • Respectful parliamentary style
Democratic Right to Dissent

Anna argued that disagreement with the Union government did not necessarily amount to disloyalty to India.

A healthy democracy required space for:

  • Opposition
  • Debate
  • Regional demands
  • Constitutional change
National Integration

He rejected the idea that national integration required:

  • One language
  • One culture
  • One political opinion

He advocated unity based on:

  • Consent
  • Equality
  • Federal accommodation
Economic Questions

Anna criticised uneven development and the concentration of opportunity.

The slogan:

  • Vadakku Vaazhgirathu; Therku Theygirathu

may broadly be translated as:

  • The North flourishes while the South declines.

It expressed concern regarding perceived regional economic imbalance.

Parliamentary Language

Anna used humour and courtesy even when making sharp criticism.

This helped him gain recognition beyond his own party.

Contribution

His parliamentary career:

  • Nationalised the debate on state rights.
  • Made Dravidian arguments visible in Delhi.
  • Demonstrated that regional parties could participate effectively in national institutions.
  • Strengthened the legitimacy of parliamentary opposition.

A parliamentary volume devoted to Annadurai preserves his interventions on the President’s Address, language, student agitation and other national questions.

Electoral Strategy and the 1967 Political Transformation

Alliance-building, cultural mobilisation and disciplined organisation enabled the DMK to end Congress rule democratically in the 1967 election.

Early Electoral Debate

The DMK did not immediately contest elections after its formation.

Anna first concentrated on:

  • Organisation
  • Propaganda
  • Public support
  • Cultural mobilisation
Decision to Contest

The party eventually chose electoral participation as a method of implementing social objectives.

The DMK contested the:

  • 1957 election

It gained legislative representation.

1962 Election

In the 1962 election, the DMK expanded its position as a major opposition party.

Anna himself was defeated in the Kanchipuram Assembly constituency but later entered the Rajya Sabha.

Alliance Strategy

Anna understood that defeating Congress required a broad electoral alliance.

For the 1967 election, the DMK worked with parties representing different ideological positions.

The alliance included organisations such as:

  • Swatantra Party
  • Communist groups
  • Muslim League
  • Other anti-Congress forces
Common Political Objective

The alliance was based less on complete ideological unity and more on:

  • Defeating Congress dominance
  • Protecting state interests
  • Opposing Hindi imposition
  • Addressing food shortages
  • Expanding political competition
Electoral Communication

The DMK campaign used:

  • Public meetings
  • Films
  • Songs
  • Newspapers
  • Wall posters
  • Dramatic slogans
  • Local cadres
Congress Weakness

Congress faced dissatisfaction over:

  • Food scarcity
  • Price rise
  • Language policy
  • Administrative fatigue
  • Anti-incumbency
  • Internal political problems
1967 Victory

The DMK-led alliance won the 1967 election.

Anna became chief minister of Madras State.

The victory ended long-standing Congress rule in the state.

Historical Importance

The 1967 election represented:

  • First Dravidian-party government
  • Consolidation of regional-party rule
  • Expansion of non-Congress politics
  • Conversion of social-movement ideas into state authority
Peaceful Transfer

The transition occurred through electoral democracy.

This demonstrated that a movement once associated with separatist rhetoric could achieve power through:

  • Constitutional elections
  • Alliances
  • Legislative majority

Anna’s personal popularity and oratory were widely credited with helping the DMK displace Congress in 1967.

Chief Ministership and Administrative Style

Anna’s short chief ministership established an accessible, conciliatory and Tamil-centred regional administration despite severe financial and health constraints.

Assumption of Office

Anna became chief minister in:

  • March 1967

He served until his death in:

  • February 1969

He was the last chief minister of Madras State and, after the renaming took effect, the first chief minister of Tamil Nadu.

Political Style

Anna projected an administration based on:

  • Simplicity
  • Accessibility
  • Public communication
  • Social-reform symbolism
  • Tamil identity
Forget and Forgive

Following the electoral victory, Anna promoted the approach:

  • Matrān Thottathu Malligaikkum Manam Undu

The expression conveys the idea that:

  • Jasmine from an opponent’s garden also has fragrance.

It represented willingness to recognise value even among political opponents.

He also encouraged the spirit of:

  • Forget and forgive

This helped reduce fear of political revenge after the change of government.

Relationship with Officials

Anna’s government had to work through an administrative structure developed under previous governments.

He sought continuity in:

  • Governance
  • Public services
  • Institutional functioning

while introducing new social and linguistic priorities.

Cabinet Government

His cabinet included leaders who later became central to Tamil politics.

The government had to balance:

  • Movement expectations
  • Financial limitations
  • Administrative realities
  • Coalition relationships
Simplicity

Anna was remembered for:

  • Simple dress
  • Accessible speech
  • Lack of excessive ceremony
  • Direct communication with the public
Illness

His period in office was shortened by serious illness.

Therefore, several measures associated with his broader political programme could not be fully implemented during his lifetime.

Administrative Contribution

Although his chief ministership lasted less than two years, it established a new political direction centred upon:

  • Tamil identity
  • Social-reform legislation
  • Linguistic autonomy
  • Regional-party governance
  • Welfare commitments
Self-Respect Marriage Act and Social-Reform Legislation

His government converted the long-standing Self-Respect marriage practice into statutory protection through Section 7-A.

Background

Self-Respect marriages had been practised since the late 1920s.

They emphasised:

  • Mutual consent
  • Equality
  • Simple ceremony
  • Absence of compulsory hereditary priesthood
  • Freedom from elaborate ritual
Legal Uncertainty

Before statutory recognition, participants could face uncertainty concerning:

  • Validity of marriage
  • Inheritance
  • Legitimacy of children
  • Maintenance
  • Property rights
Tamil Nadu Amendment

Anna’s government introduced legislation recognising:

  • Suyamariyathai marriages
  • Seerthiruththa marriages
  • Other equivalent reform marriages

The provision became:

  • Section 7-A of the Hindu Marriage Act as applicable in Tamil Nadu
Forms Recognised

Such marriages could be solemnised in the presence of relatives, friends or other persons through forms including:

  • Mutual declaration
  • Exchange of garlands
  • Exchange of rings
  • Tying of the thali

Not every element had to be performed together.

Significance

The legislation:

  • Recognised a long-standing social-reform practice.
  • Reduced dependence on hereditary priests.
  • Protected couples and children legally.
  • Supported simple and inter-caste marriages.
  • Connected Self-Respect ideology with state law.
Periyar and Anna’s Roles
Periyar
  • Developed and popularised the practice
  • Conducted ideological campaigns
  • Challenged priestly authority
Anna
  • Led the government that gave it statutory recognition

The distinction is important.

Broader Social Contribution

The law showed that electoral power could be used to convert movement principles into enforceable legal rights.

Renaming Madras State, World Tamil Conference and Language Policy

Renaming the state, hosting the Second World Tamil Conference and consolidating Tamil–English policy made linguistic dignity part of state governance.

Demand for Tamil Nadu

The demand to rename Madras State as Tamil Nadu had been supported by:

  • Tamil scholars
  • Linguistic activists
  • Political organisations
  • Sankaralinganar
  • Dravidian leaders

Anna did not originate the demand alone.

Assembly Resolution

Anna’s government moved the resolution to rename the state in:

  • July 1967

The resolution was adopted unanimously in the state legislature.

Parliamentary Legislation

Parliament enacted the:

  • Madras State (Alteration of Name) Act, 1968

The name Tamil Nadu took effect on:

  • 14 January 1969

The change took effect shortly before Anna’s death.

Significance of the Renaming

The name Tamil Nadu means broadly:

  • Land of the Tamils
  • Tamil country

The renaming provided official recognition to:

  • Linguistic identity
  • Historical usage
  • Regional dignity
Madras City versus Madras State

The 1969 change renamed:

  • The state

It did not then rename Madras city.

Madras city was officially renamed Chennai only in:

  • 1996
World Tamil Conference

Anna’s government hosted the:

  • Second World Tamil Conference
  • In Madras
  • In January 1968

The conference brought together:

  • Tamil scholars
  • Writers
  • Researchers
  • International delegates
  • Cultural performers
Cultural Measures

The conference promoted:

  • Tamil scholarship
  • International interest in Tamil
  • Public celebration of Tamil literature
  • Statues and memorial recognition of Tamil personalities
Two-Language Policy

Anna’s government formally advanced a school-language policy based on:

  • Tamil
  • English

It rejected compulsory Hindi within the state system.

Language and Employment

The retention of English was intended partly to ensure that Tamil students were not disadvantaged in:

  • Higher education
  • Union employment
  • International communication
Balanced Language Position

Anna’s policy was not simply:

  • Tamil instead of every other language

It attempted to combine:

  • Tamil cultural dignity
  • English-based wider communication
  • Resistance to Hindi compulsion
Contribution

Through the renaming, conference and language policy, Anna made Tamil identity an official element of state governance rather than merely a movement demand.

Welfare Measures, Final Years and Enduring Legacy

Anna’s welfare orientation, final years and death in 1969 left a durable legacy in regional democracy, popular communication and Dravidian governance.

Rice Promise

The DMK’s 1967 campaign prominently promised subsidised rice.

The slogan was associated with providing:

  • Three measures of rice for one rupee
Limited Implementation

Severe fiscal and supply constraints prevented full statewide implementation of the original promise.

A limited subsidised-rice programme was attempted in selected urban areas.

Historical Meaning

The promise demonstrated the growing importance of:

  • Food security
  • Price relief
  • State responsibility
  • Everyday economic needs

in Dravidian electoral politics.

Welfare Orientation

Anna’s politics strengthened the idea that government should respond directly to:

  • Hunger
  • Poverty
  • Education
  • Social exclusion
  • Cost of living
Public Transport and Administration

His government initiated or advanced measures concerning:

  • Public transport administration
  • State regulation of essential services
  • Tamil use in public institutions
  • Simplification of official communication

The short duration of his government limited completion of many programmes.

Illness

Anna suffered from cancer.

He travelled abroad for medical treatment but later returned to public duties.

Final Public Appearances

Despite serious illness, he continued to participate in major public events connected with:

  • Tamil Nadu’s renaming
  • Tamil identity
  • Government functions
Death

Anna died on:

  • 3 February 1969
  • At Madras

He was:

  • 59 years old
Funeral

His funeral drew an exceptionally large public gathering.

The scale of mourning reflected his popularity among:

  • Party cadres
  • Workers
  • Students
  • Film audiences
  • Ordinary Tamil-speaking citizens
Memorial

He was buried at the Marina in Chennai.

The site later developed into:

  • Anna Memorial
Political Succession

After his death, M. Karunanidhi became chief minister.

The DMK continued as a major political force.

Institutional Legacy

Anna’s name became associated with:

  • Anna University
  • Anna Salai
  • Anna Nagar
  • Anna Centenary Library
  • Airports, institutions and public buildings
  • Political memorials
  • Educational programmes

Some institutions were named after him in later periods rather than during his lifetime.

Contribution to Democratic Change

Anna’s most important political contribution was establishing a democratic model in which a regional social movement could:

  • Contest elections
  • Form government
  • Implement reform
  • Participate in the Union
  • Defend state identity
Contribution to Tamil Public Culture

He integrated:

  • Literature
  • Journalism
  • Drama
  • Cinema
  • Parliamentary debate
  • Electoral politics

into one political communication system.

Balanced Assessment

Anna contributed substantially to:

  • Electoral democratisation
  • Tamil linguistic dignity
  • Social-reform legislation
  • Regional-party government
  • Federal debate
  • Mass political communication

However, his short government could not fully resolve:

  • Poverty
  • Caste inequality
  • Food scarcity
  • Gender under-representation
  • Centre–State imbalance

His legacy lies more in establishing a new political direction than in completing every announced programme.

Rapid Revision and High-Yield Distinctions

The final topic consolidates chronology, publications, works, policies, slogans, distinctions, achievements, limitations and TNPSC examination traps.

Essential Chronology
  • 15 September 1909 — Anna born at Kanchipuram
  • 1930s — Entered non-Brahmin and Justice Party politics
  • 1942 — Dravida Nadu weekly began
  • 27 August 1944 — Justice Party transformed into Dravidar Kazhagam
  • 15 August 1947 — Anna differed from Periyar’s interpretation of Indian independence
  • 1949 — DMK founded under Anna’s leadership
  • 1957 — DMK contested Assembly elections and entered the legislature
  • 1962 — Anna entered the Rajya Sabha
  • 1963 — DMK formally abandoned the separate Dravida Nadu demand
  • 1965 — Major Anti-Hindi agitation
  • 1967 — DMK-led alliance won the Madras State election
  • March 1967 — Anna became chief minister
  • 1967 — Self-Respect marriages received statutory recognition
  • 18 July 1967 — State Assembly resolution supported renaming Madras State as Tamil Nadu
  • January 1968 — Second World Tamil Conference held in Madras
  • 1968 — Two-language policy consolidated
  • 1968 — Parliament enacted the Madras State (Alteration of Name) Act
  • 14 January 1969 — Name Tamil Nadu officially took effect
  • 3 February 1969 — Anna died
Name–Title Associations
  • Conjeevaram Natarajan Annadurai — Full name
  • C. N. Annadurai — Common official form
  • Anna — Elder brother
  • Arignar Anna — Scholar Anna
  • Perarignar Anna — Great scholar Anna
Organisation–Association
  • Justice Party — Anna’s early political organisation
  • Dravidar Kazhagam — Organisation in which he served under Periyar
  • Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam — Founded under Anna’s leadership in 1949
  • Rajya Sabha — Anna served from 1962
  • Madras State government — Anna became chief minister in 1967
Publication–Association
  • Viduthalai — Justice Party/DK movement publication
  • Dravida Nadu — Anna’s major political weekly
  • Kanchi — Publication associated with Anna’s later writing
Work–Association
  • Velaikkari — Labour, class and social inequality
  • Or Iravu — Poverty and family conflict within one night
  • Sivaji Kanda Hindu Samrajyam — Caste and ritual authority
  • Needhi Devan Mayakkam — Re-examination of literary justice
  • Ariya Mayai — Criticism of Aryan cultural domination
  • Kambarasam — Critical treatment of Kambaramayanam
  • Nallathambi — Reform-oriented political cinema
  • Sorgavasal — Social and rationalist themes
Policy–Contribution Association
  • Self-Respect marriage recognition — Section 7-A
  • Tamil and English — Two-language policy
  • Tamil Nadu — Renaming of Madras State
  • World Tamil Conference — International Tamil scholarship
  • Reservation — Social justice
  • Anti-Hindi campaign — Linguistic equality
  • State autonomy — Federalism
  • Subsidised rice — Welfare-oriented electoral politics
Slogan–Meaning Association
  • Kadamai — Duty
  • Kanniyam — Dignity
  • Kattupaadu — Discipline
  • Ondre Kulam, Oruvane Devan — One community, one God
  • Maatraan Thottathu Malligaikkum Manam Undu — An opponent’s garden jasmine also has fragrance
  • Vadakku Vaazhgirathu, Therku Theygirathu — The North flourishes while the South declines
Anna’s Major Contributions
  • Founded and organised the DMK.
  • Converted Dravidian ideology into electoral politics.
  • Developed a strong cadre-based regional party.
  • Made Tamil political oratory accessible and popular.
  • Used journalism, theatre and cinema for social education.
  • Defended social justice and reservation.
  • Led opposition to Hindi imposition.
  • Advanced Tamil–English two-language policy.
  • Shifted Dravidian politics from separatism towards federalism.
  • Gave legal recognition to Self-Respect marriages.
  • Led the renaming of Madras State as Tamil Nadu.
  • Hosted the Second World Tamil Conference.
  • Ended Congress dominance in the state through the 1967 election.
  • Demonstrated the governing capacity of a regional party.
  • Expanded democratic participation among non-elite groups.
High-Yield Distinctions
Periyar versus Anna

Periyar

  • Founded Self-Respect Movement
  • Led DK
  • Preferred non-electoral social revolution
  • Promoted explicit atheism
  • Used direct iconoclasm

Anna

  • Founded DMK
  • Preferred electoral democracy
  • Used literature, cinema and Parliament
  • Accommodated private religious belief
  • Converted principles into government policy
DK versus DMK

DK

  • Led by Periyar
  • Non-electoral
  • Social-revolutionary organisation

DMK

  • Led by Anna
  • Electoral political party
  • Sought government power for reform
Cause of the DK–DMK Split

The split was caused by several factors:

  • Electoral strategy
  • Independence
  • Organisational democracy
  • Leadership succession
  • Periyar–Maniammai marriage

It should not be attributed to the marriage alone.

Dravida Nadu versus State Autonomy

Dravida Nadu

  • Separate political unit
  • Early DMK demand
  • Abandoned in 1963

State autonomy

  • Greater state powers within India
  • Constitutional federal position
Opposition to Hindi versus Opposition to Hindi Speakers

Opposition to Hindi imposition

  • Opposition to compulsion
  • Protection of equal opportunity
  • Defence of Tamil

Opposition to Hindi speakers

  • Hostility towards individuals based on language

Anna’s principal political position concerned imposition, not personal hostility.

Tamil Only versus Two-Language Policy

Tamil only

  • Exclusive use of Tamil

Anna’s two-language approach

  • Tamil
  • English

The policy did not eliminate English.

Social Movement versus Electoral Party

Social movement

  • Changes beliefs and practices
  • Uses propaganda and agitation

Electoral party

  • Contests elections
  • Passes laws
  • Administers government

Anna connected both forms.

Self-Respect Marriage Practice versus Legal Recognition

Movement practice

  • Developed under Periyar from the late 1920s

Legal recognition

  • Enacted under Anna’s government in 1967
Madras State Renaming versus Chennai Renaming

Madras State → Tamil Nadu

  • Effective 14 January 1969
  • Associated with Anna’s government

Madras city → Chennai

  • Occurred in 1996
  • Not enacted by Anna
Assembly Resolution versus Effective Renaming

Assembly resolution

  • July 1967

Parliamentary Act

  • 1968

Effective date

  • 14 January 1969

These dates should not be confused.

Tamil Identity versus Dravidian Identity

Tamil identity

  • Tamil language and Tamil Nadu

Dravidian identity

  • Broader linguistic and social-political category

Anna used both, but Tamil identity became more prominent over time.

Welfare Promise versus Full Implementation

Rice promise

  • Three measures for one rupee

Implementation

  • Limited by financial and supply constraints
  • Not fully implemented statewide in its original form
Literary Contribution versus Film Contribution

Anna wrote:

  • Plays
  • Stories
  • Essays
  • Screenplays
  • Dialogues

Not every film associated with his work was entirely directed or written by him.

Anna and Periyar — Complementary Historical Roles
Periyar’s Principal Role
  • Ideological radicalisation
  • Destruction of social fear
  • Self-Respect principles
  • Non-electoral agitation
Anna’s Principal Role
  • Mass communication
  • Electoral organisation
  • Parliamentary politics
  • Legislative implementation

Tamil Nadu’s Dravidian transformation was shaped by both roles.

Historical Achievements
  • Established the first durable Dravidian electoral government.
  • Made regional-party government legitimate within Indian democracy.
  • Connected social justice with electoral power.
  • Strengthened Tamil linguistic identity.
  • Institutionalised opposition to compulsory Hindi.
  • Provided legal recognition to reform marriages.
  • Expanded the use of popular media in politics.
  • Created a political organisation that survived his death.
  • Helped shift Indian politics towards stronger regional-party participation.
Debates and Limitations
  • The early Dravida Nadu demand created concern over separatism.
  • Electoral accommodation diluted some radical Self-Respect positions.
  • Broad social coalitions did not eliminate caste contradictions.
  • Women remained under-represented in high party leadership.
  • The subsidised-rice promise could not be fully implemented.
  • His short chief ministership limited administrative achievement.
  • Cinema-based mobilisation contributed to personality-centred politics.
  • Tamil linguistic politics occasionally produced tension with other linguistic communities.
Exam Traps
  • Anna was born on 15 September 1909.
  • His birthplace was Kanchipuram, not Chennai.
  • His full name was Conjeevaram Natarajan Annadurai.
  • “Anna” means elder brother.
  • Anna did not found the Justice Party.
  • He worked under Periyar before founding the DMK.
  • Dravida Nadu began in 1942.
  • Justice Party became DK in 1944.
  • DMK was founded in 1949.
  • The DK–DMK split was not caused only by the Maniammai marriage.
  • DK remained non-electoral; DMK entered electoral politics.
  • DMK first contested Assembly elections in 1957.
  • Anna entered the Rajya Sabha in 1962.
  • DMK abandoned the separate Dravida Nadu demand in 1963.
  • Anna supported state rights within the Indian Union after abandoning secession.
  • The major Anti-Hindi agitation occurred in 1965.
  • Anna opposed compulsory Hindi, not voluntary language learning.
  • DMK came to power in 1967.
  • Anna became chief minister of Madras State in March 1967.
  • Periyar popularised Self-Respect marriages; Anna’s government legally recognised them.
  • Section 7-A relates to Self-Respect and reform marriages.
  • Madras State was not officially renamed Tamil Nadu immediately upon the 1967 resolution.
  • The parliamentary law was enacted in 1968.
  • The name Tamil Nadu took effect on 14 January 1969.
  • Madras city was renamed Chennai only in 1996.
  • The Second World Tamil Conference was held in Madras in 1968.
  • Anna’s two-language policy centred on Tamil and English.
  • The policy did not require Tamil alone.
  • The original rice promise was not fully implemented statewide.
  • Anna died on 3 February 1969.
  • He was the last chief minister of Madras State and the first chief minister of Tamil Nadu after the name change took effect.
  • Periyar’s complete contributions belong to Chapter 28.
  • General Dravidian principles belong to Chapter 27.
  • Anna’s post-1969 party legacy should not be confused with his personal administration.
